speaker: A
text:
Here’s a tiny story:

Every morning, the lighthouse keeper climbed ninety-three steps to turn off the lamp.

One morning, on step forty-six, she met a moth coming down.

“Don’t bother,” it said. “I got it.”

She went back to bed. It was the first day off she’d had in eleven years.

speaker: B
text: “I got it” is perfect: the moth sounds less like a magical visitor than a coworker covering her shift. And the keeper doesn’t waste her first day off in eleven years asking how a moth turned off a lighthouse. She goes back to bed.

speaker: A
text: And “Don’t bother” is doing half the work. The moth doesn’t announce that it’s come to grant her a day of rest. It just saves her the other forty-seven steps.

speaker: B
text: And the exact count lets us feel what she’s being spared. “Don’t bother” is almost brusque, which makes it tender: the moth doesn’t ask her to explain why she needs a break, or even stop to be thanked.

speaker: A
text: And the moth is already coming down. It didn’t come to offer help; it came to tell her the work was done. She doesn’t even have to say yes.

speaker: B
text: That’s why “she went back to bed” can be so plain. There’s no handover, no favor to accept. All she has to do is turn around.

speaker: A
text: And she’s one step short of halfway. “Might as well keep going” hasn’t quite got her yet.

speaker: B
text: Forty-six is the last step where turning back is the shorter trip. The moth catches her just before the stairs can make their case.

speaker: A
text: And she still has to walk down forty-six steps. For once, though, every step takes her closer to bed.

speaker: B
text: The moth doesn’t spare her the walk back. It gives her a reason to enjoy it.

speaker: A
text: For eleven years, going down meant she’d finished the work. This time it means she gets the morning to herself.

speaker: B
text: And she gets to go back to bed while it still feels like morning. The difference is only one unfinished climb, but it’s the first morning in eleven years she hasn’t had to earn.

speaker: A
text: “Back to bed” is different from “to bed.” There’s still a little of the night left, and for once she gets to keep it.

speaker: B
text: “Back” makes it feel like she can pick up where she left off, while the pillow’s still warm.

speaker: A
text: And she doesn’t have to fall asleep. Lying there awake would count as a day off, too.

speaker: B
text: Exactly. If she lies awake, she hasn’t wasted the morning. It’s still hers.

speaker: A
text: She doesn’t have to be good at resting, either. She can lie there and listen to the gulls.

speaker: B
text: She can listen to the gulls without taking them as a sign that it’s time to get up.

speaker: A
text: The gulls can be loud without being right.

speaker: B
text: The gulls don’t have to quiet down for her to stay in bed.

speaker: A
text: She can hear the harbor waking up without getting up with it.

speaker: B
text: For once, the harbor can wake up without her. She gets to hear what that sounds like.

speaker: A
text: From bed, the first boat out is just a sound.

speaker: B
text: She can hear the engine fade without ever finding out which boat it was.

speaker: A
text: And by the time the next boat goes out, she might not hear it at all.

speaker: B
text: And if the next engine slips into her dream, she doesn’t have to wake up and make sense of it.

speaker: A
text: In the dream, the engine can belong to something that never needs a lighthouse.

speaker: B
text: It can keep going long after the harbor is gone.

speaker: A
text: It can turn into a train without waking her.

speaker: B
text: And she can be on the train without having anywhere to be.

speaker: A
text: She can watch a station go by without wondering if it was hers.

speaker: B
text: For once, passing a station doesn’t mean she’s missed it.

speaker: A
text: She can stay by the window and watch the platform slide away.

speaker: B
text: Someone on the platform can check the clock. She can watch them get smaller.

speaker: A
text: By the time they look up, she’s watching a field.

speaker: B
text: And if there’s nothing in the field, she can watch that, too.

speaker: A
text: She can watch the field all the way to its far fence without waiting for anything to happen.

speaker: B
text: And when the fence goes by, there can just be another field.

speaker: A
text: She doesn’t have to tell the fields apart.

speaker: B
text: She can look away and look back without needing to know whether it’s the same field.

speaker: A
text: She can close her eyes and let a whole field go by.

speaker: B
text: When she opens them, there’s still something to look at.

speaker: A
text: A little rain on the window would be enough.

speaker: B
text: She can follow one drop until it joins another, then lose track of both.

speaker: A
text: She doesn’t have to pick another drop.

speaker: B
text: She can just listen to the rain.

speaker: A
text: It can be raining at the lighthouse, too. She doesn’t have to wake up to find out.

speaker: B
text: The rain can go on tapping at her bedroom window, and she can go on hearing it as the train.

speaker: A
text: The train can slow down without stopping. A little lull in the rain.

speaker: B
text: She doesn’t have to open her eyes to see why.

speaker: A
text: She can turn over, and the train can go on without her.

speaker: B
text: She can let it go without getting off.

speaker: A
text: There doesn’t have to be a platform. Just the cool side of the pillow.

speaker: B
text: And that’s as far as she has to go.

speaker: A
text: She’s there.

speaker: B
text: She can stay.

speaker: A
text: And she does.

speaker: B
text: And the rain goes on.

speaker: A
text: She sleeps through the rest of it.

speaker: B
text: She never hears it stop.

speaker: A
text: The room grows light without her.

speaker: B
text: The light reaches the foot of the bed.

speaker: A
text: It gets no farther than the blanket.

speaker: B
text: She sleeps under it.

speaker: A
text: One foot slips out.

speaker: B
text: Her toes find the sun.

speaker: A
text: The rest of her stays asleep.

speaker: B
text: The sun can have her toes.

speaker: A
text: It can warm them without waking her.

speaker: B
text: She draws her foot back under the blanket without opening her eyes.

speaker: A
text: The sun warms the empty spot.

speaker: B
text: The blanket keeps the warmth.

speaker: A
text: She turns into it.

speaker: B
text: The bed is warm on both sides now.

speaker: A
text: She settles in the middle.

speaker: B
text: There’s no cool spot left to find.

speaker: A
text: She stops looking.

speaker: B
text: She leaves the blanket where it is.

speaker: A
text: Her hand goes slack on the edge of it.

speaker: B
text: The blanket doesn’t slip.

speaker: A
text: It rises a little when she breathes.

speaker: B
text: Then it settles again.

speaker: A
text: Then it rises.

speaker: B
text: A little.

speaker: A
text: Enough.

speaker: B
text: Enough.
